toolUseResult.stdout: ## Context See proposal.md — Why, for motivation. The constraints that shape the approach: - **Obsidian assets are content-addressed and private.** `addFile` (`packages/database/src/lib/files.ts`) hashes the bytes with SHA-256, uploads them to the `assets` bucket under the hash as object name, and inserts a `FileReference` row. The bucket is not public: `storage_select_assets_access` (`supabase/schemas/assets.sql`) requires an authenticated user who passes `file_access(name)`. A browser `` tag cannot fetch these bytes. - **Roam assets are world-readable and not ours.** All 1,932 Firebase URLs in the graph export share one bucket, `firescript-577a2.appspot.com` — Roam's own Firebase project — with the path shape `imgs/app//<10-char random name>.` and a Firebase download token on 100% of them. - **Roam's upload API gives us no control over the URL.** We choose neither bucket nor path: the stored object name is a fresh random uid on every call, so the URL of an already-uploaded file cannot be derived or predicted. - **`file.upload` returns a block string, not a URL**, and its shape depends on the media type: `![](url)` for images, `{{[[pdf]]: url}}` / `{{[[audio]]: url}}` / `{{[[video]]: url}}` for those, and a bare URL for everything else. The mirror has to unwrap it to get the URL for the registry, and it means a non-image asset should be embedded with Roam's own syntax rather than the markdown `![]()` the source note used. (`roamAlphaAPI.util.uploadFile` is a legacy alias for the same call.) - **The original filename is preserved, in Firebase custom metadata.** Verified against a real upload: requesting the Storage URL with `alt=media` **stripped** returns the object descriptor as JSON, and the uploaded name is in `metadata["file-name"]` (alongside `metadata["file-type"]`): ```javascript "contentDisposition": "inline; filename*=utf-8''lqp2ioVNC3.png", "md5Hash": "REDACTED", "metadata": { "file-type": "image/png", "file-name": "CleanShot 2025-11-16 at 17.14.44@2x.png" } ``` Three consequences. It is how the publisher fills `source_path` (Decision 8), at publish time, once per asset — rather than every destination doing it per import. The read is **cheap** — a small JSON response, no bytes — which is what makes Decision 4's recovery path viable, and it bypasses the Roam API entirely. And it is invisible to `curl -I`: `contentDisposition` echoes only the storage uid, so a HEAD on the content URL yields a false negative. The descriptor also carries `md5Hash`, a content fingerprint available without downloading. - **The Roam API itself has no metadata-only read.** `file.get({url})` resolves to a `File`; with `format: "base64"`, to `{base64, filename, mimetype}`. Both transfer the content. `get` restores the name by reading `metadata["file-name"]`; where that key is absent it falls back to the storage uid, which is why Roam's own reference example shows `File {name: "GVfB6XBcMR.pdf", …}`. - `file.delete({url})` is the third operation available. - **Roam never collects uploaded files, and says so.** Its documentation: "Deleting a block doesn't delete the file that was uploaded in it. The upload stays in your graph's storage… There's no way to search for those leftover files yet." So nothing upstream will clean up after us, and orphans are undiscoverable — which independently confirms what the API surface implies. The same page notes that deleting a file runs a **reference check** telling you whether anything still displays it, and that deletion is permanent. That check is a property of Roam's own deletion flow, not something `file.delete({url})` exposes to us. - **A `FileReference` requires a published `Content`.** The table's FK targets `Content(space_id, source_local_id, variant, original)`, and `Content.document_id` is `NOT NULL`, which pulls in a `Document`, which needs an `author_id` on `PlatformAccount`. - **Roam's materialization writes nothing to Supabase.** `materializeSharedNode` only reads (`apps/roam/src/utils/materializeSharedNode.ts:137`), so an imported page has no `Concept`, `Document`, or `Content` row of its own. - **Every access helper is anchored on the current user.** `in_space` (`supabase/schemas/account.sql:277`) and `can_view_specific_resource` (`supabase/schemas/content.sql:203`) both join `my_user_accounts()`, and `file_access` is built on them. None can be evaluated for an anonymous request. - **Roam stores arbitrary JSON on pages.** `importedSourceIdentity.ts` writes structured props under `DISCOURSE_GRAPH_PROP_NAME` on a page uid and queries them across the graph with datalog (`getImportedSourceRids`). Page props survive content replacement — that is how import identity persists across refresh. - **Obsidian already skips external links on import.** `processLink` returns `http://` and `https://` link paths untouched (`apps/obsidian/src/utils/importNodes.ts:643`). ## Goals / Non-Goals **Goals:** - One asset-reference shape both directions can be described in, so the four follow-up tickets stop at implementation rather than re-deciding the payload. - Never fail a node import or a node publish because of an asset. Every asset failure degrades to the link already in the markdown, and is reported. Since the markdown is never rewritten at publish (Decision 2), that link is always still there to degrade to. - Choose deliberately between revocable and durable for mirrored bytes, and record why — this is the decision most likely to be revisited. **Non-Goals:** - Not an asset synchronization system. There is no refresh when upstream bytes change, and no deletion. - Not an access-control mechanism. Nothing here narrows or widens who can see an asset; visibility follows the referencing node's existing row-level security, or, once mirrored, follows Firebase. - Not a general blob store abstraction. Two hosts, two storage models, one narrow bridge. ## Decisions ### 1. Find assets by parsing markdown; add only the column a consumer reads - Asset references are discovered by parsing the `full` markdown content of a node. `FileReference` gains one nullable column, `source_path` (Decision 8), and nothing else. - **Why discovery stays in the markdown:** the reference token is already there, and every consumer has to parse the markdown anyway in order to rewrite links — so an index keyed on anything else would be a second copy of information nobody reads from the copy. - **A failed asset is not data anywhere, not even in the contract.** `CrossAppAsset` requires its content hash, and an asset whose bytes were not stored is represented by its absence from `CrossAppNode.assets` — not by an entry with nothing to resolve. The contract can only be built from `FileReference` rows, every one of which has a hash, so a hash-less entry would have no producer. Failure is reported by whichever transfer hit it, in that transfer's own result, and is never persisted: it belongs to the moment of copying, not to the node. - **What changed:** an earlier draft stored nothing at all, on the grounds that a row recording a Roam-origin Firebase URL would be write-only — we could not revoke those bytes, garbage-collect them, or serve them, so nothing would ever query it. That argument was about bytes we did not hold. Decision 2 now copies Roam-origin bytes into our own bucket, so a `FileReference` row is written and there **is** a reader: the destination importer resolves assets from those rows. **Alternatives considered:** - **Make `filehash` nullable and add a `url` column**, so a `FileReference` can point at bytes we deliberately never store. Still rejected, now for a sharper reason: a reference whose bytes we do not hold is not a reference, it is the degradation path, and it already has a representation — the URL left in the markdown with no row. Note this is the change that carries the trigger hazard below; Decision 8's `source_path` does not, because it leaves `filehash NOT NULL`. It also requires guarding both trigger functions in `supabase/schemas/assets.sql` — `after_delete_update_fref` would otherwise reach `INSERT INTO public.file_gc VALUES (NULL)` on any delete of a NULL-hash row, since `file_exists(NULL)` is false, and fail the delete outright. And the deferred transfer future does not need it either: downloading a Firebase asset and calling `addFile` produces an ordinary hashed row. - **Add `mimetype` and `size` columns**, backfilled from `storage.objects.metadata`. Rejected once the Vercel route (Decision 3) was set aside: the mirror path downloads the blob anyway and gets `.type` and `.size` from the response for free. Note the argument deliberately does **not** rest on Obsidian's current 6 MB publish cap (`syncDgNodesToSupabase.ts:706`), which is expected to rise — a pre-flight size check becomes worth having once large files can reach the bucket, but `storage.objects.metadata` already carries size and is readable through the storage API, so the answer is still a metadata read rather than a column. **Accepted cost:** asset enumeration requires markdown parsing, which is more expensive and less precise than a table lookup. Acceptable for v0; if a consumer ever needs enumeration without parsing, the nullable-`filehash`-plus-`url` shape above is the design to revive. ### 2. Roam-origin assets are copied into Supabase; the markdown is not rewritten - At publish time the Roam client fetches each referenced Firebase asset, hashes it, uploads it to the `assets` bucket through `addFile`, and writes a `FileReference` whose `filepath` is the Firebase URL exactly as it appears in the markdown. - **Why:** this follows the path Obsidian already uses instead of inventing a second one. A destination resolves an asset by looking up its `FileReference` and downloading from our bucket, knowing nothing about where the asset came from. Obsidian's importer already works this way; it needs `source_path` (Decision 8) and nothing else. - **Why the URL stays in the markdown:** it is the token the source page contains, exactly as a vault path is the token an Obsidian note contains. Keeping it is what lets it serve as the `FileReference` primary-key component and as the importer's `pathMapping` key (`importNodes.ts:835`). It is also the degradation path: when bytes cannot be copied no row is written, and the URL in the markdown is all a destination has. - **A destination resolves by row, never by origin.** Every importer follows the same rule — resolve a reference through its `FileReference` row when one matches the token, and leave the token unchanged only when no row matches. That covers genuinely external links, which have no row, and the URL-only fallback above. It deliberately does **not** carve out a shortcut for a Roam destination reading a Roam-origin URL it could render directly; see Decision 3. - **On the Firebase download token:** it stays in `filepath`. It governs fetchability, not identity — after publish nothing needs to fetch from Firebase — and stripping it would break the `pathMapping` match while protecting nothing, since the same URL sits in `Content.text` regardless. - **Superseded:** an earlier draft left Roam-origin assets on Firebase with no transfer and no row, reasoning that the [Roam decision note](https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/3dI5iyDAI) had accepted the URL leak, so copying bought nothing a destination could not do by following the link. ENG-1870 was reverted to require persisting the bytes. The property that draft relied on — that no code branches on origin — is restored on the destination side by Decision 8 rather than by leaving the bytes where they were. ### 3. Mirror assets into Firebase on import, choosing durability over revocability - At import time the Roam client downloads the asset from the Supabase bucket with its authenticated client and re-uploads it via `file.upload`, then rewrites the markdown link to the returned URL. - **This applies to every asset on the node, whatever its origin.** A Roam-origin asset imported into a second Roam graph therefore travels Firebase to Supabase to Firebase, and lands as a fresh blob in the destination graph's storage. - **Why not short-circuit that.** The second graph could render the origin graph's Firebase URL directly, and skipping the copy would be cheaper. Rejected for two reasons. It reintroduces origin-branching in the destination, which is what Decision 8 exists to remove — an importer would have to recognise a Firebase URL to know it may skip. And the shortcut is not free: it leaves the second graph's page depending on a blob the first graph's owner can delete, at which point the embed silently stops rendering and no bookkeeping of ours can see it. Copying is the same durable-over-revocable trade made below. Decision 4's registry bounds the cost at one round trip per asset per graph, not per import. - **Note the symmetry.** With Decision 2 the design now transfers bytes in both directions: Supabase to Firebase on import into Roam, Firebase to Supabase on publish out of Roam. They are not mirror images. This one exists because a Roam page can only point at a public URL; Decision 2 exists so a destination never has to know about Firebase at all. - **Why:** Roam renders `![](url)` as an ``, which issues an **anonymous cross-origin GET** — no `Authorization` header, and cookies are third-party. Whatever the destination markdown points at must be fetchable with no credentials. Supabase-hosted bytes have no such URL. **Alternatives considered:** - **Do what Obsidian's importer already does** (download the asset and keep a local copy, linking to it by path). This is the obvious precedent and the question gets asked every time, so it is worth answering explicitly: Obsidian's strategy works because Obsidian has a filesystem, and each half of it depends on that. - _Nowhere to put the bytes._ Obsidian writes the asset into the vault and links to it by path. A Roam page can only point at a URL; there is no local copy to make. - _The fetch is not ours to make._ Obsidian's plugin downloads with an authenticated Supabase client. In Roam the fetch is performed by the browser's `` tag, anonymously, with no auth header and no usable cookies. The private bucket is unreachable from there, so the file has to end up somewhere public. - _We do not choose the location._ Obsidian picks the vault path, so it is stable and re-import is idempotent for free: the filesystem **is** the registry, resolved by `getFirstLinkpathDest`. Roam's `file.upload` assigns a fresh random URL on every call, so what the filesystem guarantees Obsidian for nothing, Roam has to be told. - Obsidian's stored bookkeeping does not transfer either, for a related reason. `frontmatter.importedAssets` records a note's assets because the vault is where they live; here the equivalent is recomputable from the page's own blocks, so Decision 4 keeps only what is expensive to recompute. - **Serve from a Vercel route** at `/api/assets/`, backed by the private bucket, following the existing `apps/website/app/api/supabase/**` pattern. This is a genuinely strong design and the main casualty of this decision. It is better on almost every axis: no duplicate blobs, one URL per asset per graph, no consumption of the user's Roam storage quota, and — the real prize — **revocable**, at two levels. It needs a small `AssetGrant(token, grantee_space_id, filehash)` table with `UNIQUE (grantee_space_id, filehash)`, and one new space-anchored SQL helper, because as noted in Context every existing access function bottoms out in `auth.uid()` and cannot be evaluated for an anonymous `` request. - Rejected for v0 on a single trade: **irrevocable is the same property as durable.** The Vercel route makes every imported image in every Roam graph depend on a service we operate; if it stops, the images stop. Firebase-mirrored copies keep rendering if our backend goes away, the org stops paying, or the project winds down. For lab notes meant to outlive the tooling, that is the more valuable property, and the team's earlier acceptance of public Firebase URLs points the same way. - Note also what the route does **not** buy: it is not privacy. A capability URL in a Roam page is a bearer token in plaintext, readable by anyone who can read the page. It converts "public forever" into "public until revoked," which is a real gain but a narrower one than it first appears. - **Signed Supabase URLs.** Rejected: they expire, and the URL is persisted into page content that outlives any expiry. - **A Roam-side `FileReference` row**, so the mirrored URL has a home in the database. Rejected because it is blocked twice over: `file_reference_update_policy` requires `in_space(space_id, 'editor')` and the importing user is not an editor of the source Obsidian space; and the FK to `Content` would require fabricating a `Document` + `Content` + `PlatformAccount` triple for a node that was never published. A pseudo-content row to satisfy a foreign key is filling a schema-shaped hole rather than modelling anything. ### 4. Deduplicate mirrors by content hash, in one Roam graph registry One map for the whole graph, held in the block props of a block titled **"Sync Asset Registry"** on a new **`[[roam/js/discourse-graph/imported-assets]]`** page, under the existing `DISCOURSE_GRAPH_PROP_NAME` namespace. Read with `getBlockProps`, written with `setBlockPropsAsync`: ```plain text [[roam/js/discourse-graph/imported-assets]] > "Sync Asset Registry" (block props) assetRegistry { "": "", ... } ``` _Why that location:_ `[[roam/js/discourse-graph]]` is used for settings, so we will create another page. A named block rather than the page's own props keeps the namespace free for other graph-level state later; also block-less pages can get reaped. The accessor creates the page and block when it is absent. - Before uploading, look up the hash and reuse the URL if present. **Order of operations on import or re-sync:** 1. Build the new markdown; collect the hashes it references. 2. For each hash — if `assetRegistry` has it, reuse the URL. Otherwise upload, then record `hash -> url`. 3. Rewrite the links and replace the page content. 4. Report what changed, if the sync surfaces a summary. **Why a registry at all:** `file.upload` is not idempotent. Without a memo, an asset referenced by three imported nodes becomes three Firebase blobs at three URLs, and every re-import adds another. Supabase already deduplicates by hash — one blob, N `FileReference` rows under different `filepath`s — so the mirror must key on **hash, not reference**, or it re-inflates what the bucket collapsed. Note this is about **not creating** garbage, which is a separate concern from collecting it (Decision 6). - **Why the key is (graph, hash):** per-graph is inherent, since `file.upload` writes into the importing graph's own `imgs/app//` folder. Cross-graph duplication is therefore not avoidable and is arguably correct. - **Name every upload `imported-.`.** - Verified end to end: uploading a `File` named `imported-deadbeef.txt` and calling `file.get` on the returned URL yields `name: imported-deadbeef.txt`, and the name is separately readable from `metadata["file-name"]` without downloading the bytes (see Context). - That makes the registry a **cache, not a source of truth** — and it is what allows this decision to store one map instead of three. The underlying facts live elsewhere and stay recoverable: ```plain text which URLs a page references -> the page's own blocks which asset a URL holds -> the file's own name assetRegistry = cache of a graph-wide scan (datalog for firebase URLs, resolve each) ``` - So a lost or stale registry costs a rebuild, not data. It is kept because recomputing it on every sync would mean a graph scan plus one metadata request per asset — worth caching, not worth treating as authoritative. - **Why the filename does not replace the registry:** deduplication asks "do I already hold this hash?" A name is only readable once you already have the URL, so answering from filenames alone means rebuilding the whole map every sync. The direction is wrong for the question; the filename is what makes the rebuild cheap, not what makes it unnecessary. - **Label non-image links with the source filename.** - `file.upload` returns a bare URL for anything that is not an image, PDF, audio or video, and a bare URL in a Roam block renders as a link whose visible text **is** the URL — a hundred-odd characters of storage uid that tells the reader nothing. The rewriting step must therefore emit `[report.docx](url)`, taking the label from the source markdown's display text or the basename of its path, rather than dropping the returned URL in raw. The name is otherwise never surfaced anywhere in Roam: images render as images, media types render in a viewer, and `metadata["file-name"]` is read by nothing in the Roam UI. This link label is the only place a user ever sees what an imported file is called. (The bare-URL rendering is inferred from the reference, not observed — confirm against a real graph.) **Alternatives considered:** - **A Supabase table keyed `(grantee_space_id, filehash)`.** Rejected for v0: it is server state for what is really client-side graph bookkeeping, and graph props keep working if the user stops using our backend. Accepted consequence: the registry is only visible to a Roam client with that graph open, so any future migration or deduplication pass must run client-side, in-graph. - **A per-page `importedAssets` list**, mirroring Obsidian's `frontmatter.importedAssets`. Its only consumer was the dropped-asset diff, and Decision 6 no longer performs one eagerly. The same list is recomputable page-locally by reading the blocks before `replace-page-content` destroys them, so persisting it bought nothing that reading does not. ### 5. Upload first, then record Record `hash -> url` after the upload returns. **Why not the reverse:** writing a placeholder before uploading was intended to make a crash between the two detectable. It does not help. The placeholder carries no URL, so a later sync can neither reuse the upload nor locate it — the outcome is a re-upload either way — and the stranded file is undiscoverable regardless, since Roam exposes no way to list a graph's files. The extra write buys a flag nothing can act on. **Accepted cost:** a crash between upload and record leaves one orphaned file. It is invisible, permanent, and harmless apart from quota. This is the same class of residue Roam's own documentation treats as normal. ### 6. Do not track garbage collection; derive it if it is ever wanted No candidate list, no dropped-asset diff, no retention bookkeeping. Our code never calls `file.delete`. **Why nothing is lost by not tracking:** because the hash is in the filename, a cleanup worklist is **derivable at any future date** — scan imported pages for firebase URLs, resolve each name to a hash, compare against what those pages currently reference. Accumulating that list eagerly forecloses nothing and costs a field, a diff, and a cross-page query on every sync for a cleanup that may never be run. **Why our code must not delete regardless:** references escape. The moment a user copies an imported image into a note of their own, that reference is invisible to any bookkeeping we could do, and deleting the blob breaks **their** page. Roam's documentation confirms deletion is permanent and that a stale embed simply stops rendering. **Who would do a cleanup, if one is ever wanted:** a person, not our code. Roam's file deletion flow runs a graph-wide reference check before confirming — exactly the visibility we lack, since it can see notes the user wrote themselves. So the route is: derive the worklist on demand, a human works through it in Roam's UI, and Roam's own check is the safety net. **Why leaving files behind is acceptable:** Roam does not collect them either, and says so — "Deleting a block doesn't delete the file that was uploaded in it. The upload stays in your graph's storage." Orphaned uploads are a normal, tolerated condition in this host, not a defect we are introducing. **The two directions are not symmetric.** Everything above is about blobs we push into Roam's Firebase storage, which nothing can collect. Roam-origin copies going the other way (Decision 2) land in Supabase and enter the existing collection path automatically: delete the node, the `FileReference` goes with it, `after_delete_update_fref` fires, and the hash reaches `file_gc` if no reference remains. That side needs no new bookkeeping because it already has some. **Note:** Supabase-side garbage collection is unaffected and needs nothing from the importer. When the Obsidian publisher removes an embed, `syncPublishedNodeAssets` deletes the `FileReference`, `after_delete_update_fref` fires, and the hash lands in `file_gc` if no reference remains. That path is already complete. ### 7. No `accessScope` field on the contract ENG-1864's acceptance criteria name an access scope. The contract does not carry one. **Why:** read access is already fully determined elsewhere — `my_file_references` joins `my_accessible_resources()`, and the bucket policy calls `file_access(name)`. An asset is exactly as visible as the node referencing it. A per-asset scope column would be a second, weaker copy of that rule, and if the two ever disagreed the row-level security one would win silently. The only other reading — "these bytes are reachable without our auth" — is both derivable from whether a URL exists and unenforceable, since we cannot change the readability of someone else's bucket. **Decision 2 makes this stronger, not weaker.** ENG-1870's restored criterion — bytes "persisted with the node's access scope" — is now satisfied by construction rather than by a field: a `FileReference` hangs off the node's `Content` row, so it is reachable exactly when the node is. A per-asset scope column would still be the weaker duplicate it always was. **What would be worth a field, if the picture changed:** publisher intent — may this asset be mirrored to a public host at all? Checkable at the point the mirroring code runs. Not in v0: with the disclosure accepted, nothing would read it. ### 8. A nullable `source_path` column, so the destination stays origin-agnostic - `FileReference` gains `source_path`, nullable, not part of the primary key. The publisher fills it; the importer's rule is **use `source_path` when present, otherwise decompose `filepath`**. - **Why now rather than after v0:** without it, an importer handed a Roam-origin row has to recognise a Firebase URL by its shape, strip `alt=media`, fetch the object descriptor and read Roam's own `metadata["file-name"]` key. That is provenance detection in the destination, and it puts Roam knowledge inside the Obsidian plugin — the one thing the shared contract exists to prevent. - **It is not only cosmetic.** `filepath` for a Roam-origin row is a URL, and the importer derives its vault path from `filepath` by splitting on `/` and sanitising each segment (`importNodes.ts:896-901`). A URL run through that becomes a deep nonsense directory. `source_path` is what keeps a URL out of the path derivation, so the origin branch it would otherwise need is not avoided by postponing — only relocated. - **Delay is one-way.** Assets imported before the column keep opaque names, and renaming them afterwards breaks links users wrote themselves. The database backfill would be easy; the vault cannot be corrected. - **Prerequisite: the importer must disambiguate colliding filenames.** This is not a latent bug being made likelier — the column introduces the exposure. An Obsidian `filepath` is a vault path, unique by construction. Roam has no asset hierarchy at all (`imgs/app//.`), so `source_path` is a bare leaf name with no uniqueness guarantee, and in practice many will be `image.png`. The current importer resolves a target-path clash by overwriting under an mtime check, with no suffixing. - **Safe by construction:** `source_path` is a plain nullable attribute. Uniqueness still rides on `filepath`; the garbage-collection triggers, `file_access`, and the bucket policy all key on `filehash` and are untouched. This is specifically **not** the change Decision 1 rejected — that one made `filehash` nullable, which is what would send `NULL` into `file_gc`. - **Post-v0:** rename `filepath`, which has held a path-or-URL since Decision 2, to something that says so — `source_ref` or `path_or_url`. One migration, both columns. ### 9. One explicit size cap per direction, 6 MiB each - `MAX_PUBLISHED_ASSET_BYTES` and `MAX_IMPORTED_ASSET_BYTES` (`packages/database/src/lib/assetLimits.ts`), both 6 MiB, tested with `isAssetTooLarge`. The boundary is inclusive, and an asset at or above the cap is skipped and reported while its node publishes or imports normally, with its token left in the markdown — the ordinary degradation path. - **Why 6 MiB on the publish side:** it is Supabase's threshold for a standard upload, above which an uploader is expected to switch to a resumable one, which `addFile` does not implement. content.text:
## Implementing: cross-app-asset-references (schema: spec-driven)

**Task 6.1 — degradation path across both directions ✓**

New file `apps/roam/src/utils/__tests__/assetDegradation.test.ts`. It runs the real `publishNodeAssets` and the real `importNodeAssets` against one shared fake Supabase store, so the rows and markdown that pass between the two halves are the actual ones, not fixtures. Only the two real network boundaries are stubbed: Roam storage (`fetch`) and `mirrorAssetToRoamStorage`.

Three cases, on a node embedding a readable asset, an unreadable one, an over-cap one, and an external link:

1. Publication leaves `MARKDOWN` byte-identical, records a row only for the readable asset, and reports the other two split into `failed` / `tooLarge`.
2. Importing that same published markdown mirrors only the asset that has a row; the unreadable and over-cap tokens and the external link arrive untouched, and the node body (heading, bullet) is intact.
3. When mirroring fails on the way in, the markdown comes back exactly as published and the failure is in `report.failed` keyed by the token.

3 tests pass; `tsc --noEmit` on `apps/roam` is clean; prettier applied.

One thing I noticed but did not touch: `publishNodeAssets.test.ts` has `describe("summarizeAssetResults")` twice (lines 462 and 538) with three identically-named tests duplicated between them — looks like an accidental paste when 2.5 landed on top of 2.4.

**Progress: 22/23.** Remaining is 6.2, `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` then `pnpm ci:validate` from the root — a long run that rewrites `node_modules`. Say the word and I'll run it.

proposal.md:5:Four follow-up tickets (ENG-1870, ENG-1871, ENG-1872, ENG-1873) each touch asset handling from a different side. Without one settled answer to "what is an asset reference, and what does each side do with one," each will invent its own payload shape and its own fallback behavior, and the two directions will diverge in ways that are expensive to reconcile later.
proposal.md:15:- **No `accessScope` field**, despite ENG-1864's wording. Read access is already fully determined by row-level security on the referencing node; a per-asset scope field would be a weaker duplicate of it. See design.md — Decision 7.
proposal.md:37:- A nullable `filename` column on `FileReference`, added to the `my_file_references` select list, with a `filename` parameter on `addFile` threaded into both the insert and the duplicate-key update (ENG-2229). Every other column considered turned out to have no consumer.
proposal.md:41:- Asset detection in published markdown, and copying those bytes into Supabase with a `FileReference` recorded against the node (ENG-1870).
proposal.md:42:- Mirror-on-import and the graph-level asset registry (ENG-1872). This is where nearly all the new code lives.
proposal.md:46:- Naming imported assets from `filename` when present and decomposing `filepath` otherwise, plus disambiguating colliding target paths (ENG-2230). This ships **with** ENG-1870, not after it: Roam's asset namespace is flat, so publication landing alone would put colliding, uncorrectable names into vaults.
proposal.md:47:- Otherwise validation (ENG-1871, ENG-1873). `syncPublishedNodeAssets` and `importNodes` are expected to satisfy the rest of the contract as they stand.
proposal.md:62:Re-cut before implementation started. ENG-2229 (the `filename` column and `addFile` signature) blocks everything and is done. ENG-2230 carries the Obsidian naming rule and must ship with ENG-1870. ENG-1872 was retitled "Copy shared assets into Roam on import", is origin-neutral, and became a parent of four children: ENG-2216 registry accessor, ENG-2218 copy one asset, ENG-2217 link rewriter, ENG-2219 materialization stage, which carries the live-graph verification. ENG-1873 likely reduces to writing a test.
design.md:66:- **Superseded:** an earlier draft left Roam-origin assets on Firebase with no transfer and no row, reasoning that the [Roam decision note](https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/3dI5iyDAI) had accepted the URL leak, so copying bought nothing a destination could not do by following the link. ENG-1870 was reverted to require persisting the bytes. The property that draft relied on — that no code branches on origin — is restored on the destination side by Decision 8 rather than by leaving the bytes where they were.
design.md:159:ENG-1864's acceptance criteria name an access scope. The contract does not carry one.
design.md:163:**Decision 2 makes this stronger, not weaker.** ENG-1870's restored criterion — bytes "persisted with the node's access scope" — is now satisfied by construction rather than by a field: a `FileReference` hangs off the node's `Content` row, so it is reachable exactly when the node is. A per-asset scope column would still be the weaker duplicate it always was.

{"id":"ENG-1873","uuid":"eea0ea74-bcc5-4d09-8f67-deb477758c7f","title":"Validate Obsidian asset import and link rewrite with Roam-origin nodes","description":"## Problem

* Obsidian asset import and markdown link rewrite need validation with Roam-origin shared asset references.
* Unresolved assets should not fail the whole node import.
* `updateMarkdownAssetLinks` has three branches: wikilinks, `[text](path)` and `![alt](path)`. It has no branch for a bare URL. Roam's `file.upload` returns a bare URL for anything that is not an image, PDF, audio or video, so a `.docx`, `.csv` or `.zip` attached to a Roam node is recorded at publish and then never rewritten at import. The note keeps pointing at Roam's storage.

## Solution

* Run the existing Obsidian asset import/link rewrite helpers against Roam-origin shared-node fixtures or test data.
* Validate resolvable assets, URL-only fallbacks, missing assets, and rewritten markdown links.
* Capture gaps as follow-up tickets rather than creating a new Obsidian asset importer.
* Add the missing bare-URL branch. Rewrite a bare Roam-storage URL that matches a reference row into a markdown link to the local copy, labelled from `source_path`, and leave a bare URL with no matching row exactly as written.

## Done When

* A Roam-origin markdown node with a resolvable asset imports into Obsidian with working links.
* URL-only or unresolved assets are preserved or reported without failing the node import.
* Existing Obsidian asset helpers are reused where practical.
* A Roam node with a non-media attachment, which Roam writes as a bare URL, imports with a working link to the local file.
* That link reads as the file's name rather than as a storage URL.
* A bare URL that is not a Roam storage URL is left untouched, including in a note that also carries assets which are rewritten.

## Out of Scope

* Roam source asset publication implementation.
* Roam asset materialization.
* Automatic asset refresh.

## Notes

* Functional requirements: [F11: Destination asset import and link rewrite](<https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/j3AqDVwfU>), [F10: Source asset publication](<https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/D-7HqQmKp>).
* Depends on [ENG-1864](<https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/issue/ENG-1864/define-cross-app-asset-reference-contract>) and [ENG-1870](<https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/issue/ENG-1870/detect-and-report-asset-references-in-roam-origin-shared-nodes>).
* Reuse current Obsidian asset import/link rewrite helpers where possible.
* The bare-URL branch is the Obsidian mirror of the Roam-side task "label a non-media link with its recorded name", and of the [Decision 4](<https://roamresearch.com/#/app/discourse-graphs/page/kd6Wpn_VF>) bullet "label non-image links with the source filename". The two directions should agree: a bare storage URL is an asset, and the name is the only thing a reader ever sees, since neither app surfaces the stored name anywhere else.
* Matching a bare URL is safe against false positives. `isRoamStorageUrl` parses with `URL` and checks the host and the bucket, so it cannot catch an ordinary hyperlink a user wrote.
* This item is implementation rather than validation, unlike the rest of the ticket. {"id":"ENG-2219","uuid":"a34e7f85-e5cd-468f-ac9c-6464a1ed83a5","title":"Add an asset copy stage to Roam node materialization","description":"## Problem

* The registry, the copy step, and the link rewriter do nothing until materialization calls them.
* An asset that fails to copy must not stop a node from importing.

## Solution

* Add a materialization stage between fetch-content and replace-page-content that copies assets and rewrites links.
* Keep the original link text for an asset that fails, and return the failure in the materialization result.

## Done When

* An Obsidian-origin node with an image imports into Roam, and the image renders. Verified in a real Roam graph, not only in unit tests: nothing in the sibling sub-issues needs a live graph, so this is the first point where the whole path is exercised against one.
* A Roam-origin node with an image imports into a second Roam graph, and the image renders from that graph's own storage.

`ci:validate` is `turbo check-types && turbo run test:unit`. The `&&` means `check-types` failing (website) short-circuited before any test ran.

Not included: `packages/database`'s `test` script (the cucumber suite that wipes the DB) and `apps/website`'s `test:integration`. So the database *unit* tests run; the database *integration* tests don't.

Yes, I'll wait on the archive operation. Ok, now I'm applying code review to ENG-2216 (Task 4.1). I switched back to that branch. Here are the findings:
1. apps/roam/src/utils/assetRegistry.ts:44 — getOrCreateRegistryBlockUid can create duplicate registry blocks under concurrency.
The existence check and the create are separated by an await, with no lock or in-flight promise memo. The realistic caller is an import mirroring several assets in parallel (publishNodeAssets.ts:277 already batches). On a fresh graph all N calls see no page, so N pages/blocks get created; findRegistryBlockUid then returns whichever getShallowTreeByParentUid yields first, so entries written to the other blocks become invisible and those assets are re-uploaded next import. A module-level let pending: Promise<string> | undefined memo around the create closes it.

2. apps/roam/src/utils/assetRegistry.ts:88 — recordMirroredAsset is a non-atomic read-modify-write, so concurrent calls lose entries.
Two concurrent calls for hashes A and B both read the pre-write map; the second block.update to land overwrites the first. The JSDoc — "Merges into the props read back at call time so a concurrent write to another key is not dropped" — holds only for a different top-level prop key (that merge is inside setBlockPropsAsync), not for two concurrent recordMirroredAsset calls, which is the common case. Either serialize writes through one promise chain, or fix the comment so it doesn't over-promise.

3. apps/roam/src/utils/assetRegistry.ts:37 — the registry is located by block text, so editing the block silently orphans it.
findRegistryBlockUid matches text === "Sync Asset Registry" on a user-visible, user-editable page. A rename or stray edit makes the next write create a second registry block; the old props stay on the graph but unreachable, and every previously mirrored asset is re-uploaded with no warning. Suggested: console.warn when the page exists but no block matches, or store the props on the page uid itself, as importedSourceIdentity.ts does.

4. apps/roam/src/utils/assetRegistry.ts:81 — readMirroredAssetUrl re-reads the whole registry per lookup.
Each call does a page-uid pull, a getShallowTreeByParentUid, and a props pull, then rebuilds a filtered copy of the entire map for one hash. A per-asset loop over N assets pays 3N graph reads. Hoisting one readAssetRegistry() into the caller (or memoizing per import run) is worth settling before the first caller lands.

5. apps/roam/src/utils/assetRegistry.ts:88 — no invalidation path for stale URLs.
If a user deletes the mirrored file from Roam storage, the hash→URL entry survives and callers get a dead URL embedded into freshly imported blocks as a broken image. There is no removal export, so a caller that sees a 404 cannot repair the registry. Cheapest to add while the module is still unused.

6. apps/roam/src/utils/assetRegistry.ts:31 — isJsonObject duplicates importedSourceIdentity.ts:15 (identical body, parameter type widened to json | undefined). Per AGENTS.md it belongs next to the json type in getBlockProps.ts, imported by both.

7. apps/roam/src/utils/__tests__/assetRegistry.test.ts:33 — the test assigns globalThis.window in beforeEach and never restores it. Harmless under Vitest's default per-file isolation, but it's the only file in src/utils/__tests__ doing an unguarded global assignment with no afterEach; the fake roamAlphaAPI would leak if isolation is disabled or the file is merged into another suite.

No correctness bugs in the pure read path: registryFromProps guards both nesting levels and filters non-string values, readAssetRegistry genuinely does not mutate the graph, and the props merge preserves sibling discourse-graph keys.

One caveat on findings 1 and 2 that the reviewer did not have: ENG-2216 explicitly says "Two clients in the same graph can write at once. The last write wins, and the cost is one redundant upload. Do not add locking." That covers cross-client races, not the single-process Promise.all case both findings describe — so finding 1 (duplicate blocks, which orphans entries permanently) is still worth fixing, and finding 2 is arguably already the accepted trade-off, leaving just the JSDoc to correct.

# Code Review Reception

## Overview

Code review requires technical evaluation, not emotional performance.

**Core principle:** Verify before implementing. Ask before assuming. Technical correctness over social comfort.

## The Response Pattern

```
WHEN receiving code review feedback:

1. READ: Complete feedback without reacting
2. UNDERSTAND: Restate requirement in own words (or ask)
3. VERIFY: Check against codebase reality
4. EVALUATE: Technically sound for THIS codebase?
5. RESPOND: Technical acknowledgment or reasoned pushback
6. IMPLEMENT: One item at a time, test each
```

## Forbidden Responses

**NEVER:**
- "You're absolutely right!" (explicit instruction-file violation)
- "Great point!" / "Excellent feedback!" (performative)
- "Let me implement that now" (before verification)

**INSTEAD:**
- Restate the technical requirement
- Ask clarifying questions
- Push back with technical reasoning if wrong
- Just start working (actions > words)

## Handling Unclear Feedback

```
IF any item is unclear:
  STOP - do not implement anything yet
  ASK for clarification on unclear items

WHY: Items may be related. Partial understanding = wrong implementation.
```

**Example:**
```
your human partner: "Fix 1-6"
You understand 1,2,3,6. Unclear on 4,5.

❌ WRONG: Implement 1,2,3,6 now, ask about 4,5 later
✅ RIGHT: "I understand items 1,2,3,6. Need clarification on 4 and 5 before proceeding."
```

## Source-Specific Handling

### From your human partner
- **Trusted** - implement after understanding
- **Still ask** if scope unclear
- **No performative agreement**
- **Skip to action** or technical acknowledgment

### From External Reviewers
```
BEFORE implementing:
  1. Check: Technically correct for THIS codebase?
  2. Check: Breaks existing functionality?
  3. Check: Reason for current implementation?
  4. Check: Works on all platforms/versions?
  5. Check: Does reviewer understand full context?

IF suggestion seems wrong:
  Push back with technical reasoning

IF can't easily verify:
  Say so: "I can't verify this without [X]. Should I [investigate/ask/proceed]?"

IF conflicts with your human partner's prior decisions:
  Stop and discuss with your human partner first
```

**your human partner's rule:** "External feedback - be skeptical, but check carefully"

## YAGNI Check for "Professional" Features

```
IF reviewer suggests "implementing properly":
  grep codebase for actual usage

  IF unused: "This endpoint isn't called. Remove it (YAGNI)?"
  IF used: Then implement properly
```

**your human partner's rule:** "You and reviewer both report to me. If we don't need this feature, don't add it."

## Implementation Order

```
FOR multi-item feedback:
  1. Clarify anything unclear FIRST
  2. Then implement in this order:
     - Blocking issues (breaks, security)
     - Simple fixes (typos, imports)
     - Complex fixes (refactoring, logic)
  3. Test each fix individually
  4. Verify no regressions
```

## When To Push Back

Push back when:
- Suggestion breaks existing functionality
- Reviewer lacks full context
- Violates YAGNI (unused feature)
- Technically incorrect for this stack
- Legacy/compatibility reasons exist
- Conflicts with your human partner's architectural decisions

**How to push back:**
- Use technical reasoning, not defensiveness
- Ask specific questions
- Reference working tests/code
- Involve your human partner if architectural

**If you're uncomfortable pushing back out loud:** Name that tension, then tell your partner about the issue you've seen. They'll appreciate your honesty.

## Acknowledging Correct Feedback

When feedback IS correct:
```
✅ "Fixed. [Brief description of what changed]"
✅ "Good catch - [specific issue]. Fixed in [location]."
✅ [Just fix it and show in the code]

❌ "You're absolutely right!"
❌ "Great point!"
❌ "Thanks for catching that!"
❌ "Thanks for [anything]"
❌ ANY gratitude expression
```

**Why no thanks:** Actions speak. Just fix it. The code itself shows you heard the feedback.

**If you catch yourself about to write "Thanks":** DELETE IT. State the fix instead.

## Gracefully Correcting Your Pushback

If you pushed back and were wrong:
```
✅ "You were right - I checked [X] and it does [Y]. Implementing now."
✅ "Verified this and you're correct. My initial understanding was wrong because [reason]. Fixing."

❌ Long apology
❌ Defending why you pushed back
❌ Over-explaining
```

State the correction factually and move on.

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake | Fix |
|---------|-----|
| Performative agreement | State requirement or just act |
| Blind implementation | Verify against codebase first |
| Batch without testing | One at a time, test each |
| Assuming reviewer is right | Check if breaks things |
| Avoiding pushback | Technical correctness > comfort |
| Partial implementation | Clarify all items first |
| Can't verify, proceed anyway | State limitation, ask for direction |

## Real Examples

**Performative Agreement (Bad):**
```
Reviewer: "Remove legacy code"
❌ "You're absolutely right! Let me remove that..."
```

**Technical Verification (Good):**
```
Reviewer: "Remove legacy code"
✅ "Checking... build target is 10.15+, this API needs 13+. Need legacy for backward compat. Current impl has wrong bundle ID - fix it or drop pre-13 support?"
```

**YAGNI (Good):**
```
Reviewer: "Implement proper metrics tracking with database, date filters, CSV export"
✅ "Grepped codebase - nothing calls this endpoint. Remove it (YAGNI)? Or is there usage I'm missing?"
```

**Unclear Item (Good):**
```
your human partner: "Fix items 1-6"
You understand 1,2,3,6. Unclear on 4,5.
✅ "Understand 1,2,3,6. Need clarification on 4 and 5 before implementing."
```

## GitHub Thread Replies

When replying to inline review comments on GitHub, reply in the comment thread (`gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pr}/comments/{id}/replies`), not as a top-level PR comment.

content.text:
Fixed 3, pushing back on 3, and one question. Full roam suite: 30 files / 224 tests pass; `tsc --noEmit` clean.

**First, a premise check that changes findings 1, 2 and 4.** The reviewer's evidence for concurrency is wrong: `publishNodeAssets.ts:277` is `summarizeAssetResults`, a synchronous reducer, and the publish path never touches the registry. Nothing in `src/` calls this module at all on this branch — the only importer is its test. The caller that eventually arrives, `importNodeAssets` on eng-2219, loops sequentially and says why: *"Sequential on purpose… the registry is what stops the second one uploading again; running them together would race that check."* So there is no in-process `Promise.all` today, and the one code path that will exist is deliberately serialized.

### Fixed

- **2 — JSDoc over-promised.** Replaced. It now says what the merge actually guarantees (sibling keys under `DISCOURSE_GRAPH_PROP_NAME` survive, because props are re-read), and states plainly that overlapping writes keep the last entry, costing one redundant upload, which is what ENG-2216 priced in.
- **6 — duplicated `isJsonObject`.** Moved to `getBlockProps.ts` next to the `json` type, typed `json | undefined` so it serves both call sites; `assetRegistry.ts` and `importedSourceIdentity.ts` now import it. (`apps/roam` sets `noUncheckedIndexedAccess: false`, so the widened parameter is defensive, not required.)
- **7 — unrestored global.** `afterEach` restores the prior `globalThis.window`, with a comment on why it matters only if isolation is off.

### Not fixed, with reasoning

- **1 — module-level promise memo.** It would guard a caller that doesn't exist, and it cannot guard the case the reviewer's scenario actually describes on a real graph: two tabs are two processes, and a per-module memo is invisible across them. That said, the reviewer is right that the *consequence* is mispriced — ENG-2216 accepted "one redundant upload", not entries that become permanently unreachable. The fix that covers both processes is on the read side, not the write side: have `findRegistryBlockUid` merge props from **every** block matching the text instead of taking `.find()`'s first. Cheap, no locking, and it makes duplicates self-healing. Want that?
- **4 — 3N reads per import.** These are local synchronous datalog pulls, N is assets-per-node, and there is no caller to measure. When one lands it can hoist a single `readAssetRegistry()`. Fixing it now is speculative.
- **5 — no invalidation export.** Nothing can detect a dead URL today, so the export would be unused on arrival. The module header already documents the registry as a rebuildable cache (uploads are named `imported-<sha256>`), so recovery is a rebuild, not a missing API. Better as a follow-up when a caller sees the 404.

### Needs your call

**3 — located by block text.** Real, and it shares a root cause with 1: the registry is addressed by a user-editable string. Two ways out:

- **A. `console.warn`** when the page exists but no block matches — cheap, keeps the shape the proposal describes, still silently re-uploads.
- **B. Store the props on the page uid**, as `importedSourceIdentity.ts` does. No text match, no duplicate block, no orphaning — it dissolves 1 and 3 together. But it drops the named block, which `proposal.md` specifies, so it's an artifact change, not just a code one.

Related: the proposal says the map lives on a block on `[[roam/js/discourse-graph]]`, while the code uses a dedicated page, `roam/js/discourse-graph/imported-assets`. That drift predates this review and wants reconciling either way.

content.content:
10:- **Roam-origin assets are copied into Supabase at publish.** The Roam client fetches each referenced Firebase asset, hashes it, and stores it through `addFile`, writing a `FileReference` whose `filepath` is the URL exactly as the markdown holds it. The markdown itself is never rewritten, so that URL stays available as the degradation path. See design.md — Decision 2.
13:- **No garbage-collection bookkeeping at all.** Our code never deletes a mirrored file, and nothing tracks which ones fell out of use: because the content hash is in the filename, a cleanup worklist is derivable at any later date, so tracking it eagerly forecloses nothing. Roam does not collect these files either, and documents that.
14:- **One additive schema change:** a nullable `filename` on `FileReference`, so a destination can name an imported asset without inspecting `filepath` for provenance. Everything else considered is still rejected: no nullable `filehash`, no `url` column, no `mimetype`/`size` columns, no trigger changes, no backfill. See design.md — Decisions 1 and 8.
37:- A nullable `filename` column on `FileReference`, added to the `my_file_references` select list, with a `filename` parameter on `addFile` threaded into both the insert and the duplicate-key update (ENG-2229). Every other column considered turned out to have no consumer.
46:- Naming imported assets from `filename` when present and decomposing `filepath` otherwise, plus disambiguating colliding target paths (ENG-2230). This ships **with** ENG-1870, not after it: Roam's asset namespace is flat, so publication landing alone would put colliding, uncorrectable names into vaults.
62:Re-cut before implementation started. ENG-2229 (the `filename` column and `addFile` signature) blocks everything and is done. ENG-2230 carries the Obsidian naming rule and must ship with ENG-1870. ENG-1872 was retitled "Copy shared assets into Roam on import", is origin-neutral, and became a parent of four children: ENG-2216 registry accessor, ENG-2218 copy one asset, ENG-2217 link rewriter, ENG-2219 materialization stage, which carries the live-graph verification. ENG-1873 likely reduces to writing a test.

Two small things I noticed in the new code, neither blocking:

1. apps/roam/src/utils/assetRegistry.ts:37 — the warn sits in findRegistryBlockUid, which readMirroredAssetUrl calls once per lookup. A per-asset loop on an orphaned registry logs the same paragraph N times. If finding 4's hoist happens in the caller it collapses on its own; otherwise a module-level hasWarned flag would.

content.text:
Both fixed, plus a third thing the second one exposed.

**1 — N warnings per import.** The warning is now behind `hasWarnedOrphanedRegistry`, cleared whenever a read finds the block. Once per *episode*, not once per session: a registry orphaned, repaired, then orphaned again says so both times, which is true both times. Independent of whether the caller ever hoists.

**2 — wrong tense on the write path.** `findRegistryBlockUid` is now `locateRegistry`, returning `{ pageUid, blockUid }` and warning about neither. `readAssetRegistry` warns; `getOrCreateRegistryBlockUid` doesn't, with a comment saying why — it repairs what it found missing in that same call. The message dropped "It will be recreated on the next import" for "Anything recorded there is lost", which is true on both paths. That restructure also removed a redundant `getPageUidByPageTitle` the create path was making.

**3 — a real warning leaking into test output.** The pre-existing "ignores a block on the page that is not the registry block" test sets up exactly the orphan condition, so it was writing the paragraph to stderr on every run. The default reporter hides it; `--reporter=verbose` shows it. Muted there with a spy that says it's incidental, and `afterEach` now calls `vi.restoreAllMocks()` so no `spyOn` outlives its test.

The two warning tests are self-contained — the first establishes and reads back a healthy registry before orphaning it, so it doesn't care what earlier tests did to the flag.

`tsc --noEmit` exits 0; 30 files / 227 tests pass, and `--reporter=verbose` shows no stray stderr.

content.content: 5:- **Obsidian assets are content-addressed and private.** `addFile` (`packages/database/src/lib/files.ts`) hashes the bytes with SHA-256, uploads them to the `assets` bucket under the hash as object name, and inserts a `FileReference` row. The bucket is not public: `storage_select_assets_access` (`supabase/schemas/assets.sql`) requires an authenticated user who passes `file_access(name)`. A browser `` tag cannot fetch these bytes. 7:- **Roam's upload API gives us no control over the URL.** We choose neither bucket nor path: the stored object name is a fresh random uid on every call, so the URL of an already-uploaded file cannot be derived or predicted. 8:- **`file.upload` returns a block string, not a URL**, and its shape depends on the media type: `![](url)` for images, `{{[[pdf]]: url}}` / `{{[[audio]]: url}}` / `{{[[video]]: url}}` for those, and a bare URL for everything else. The mirror has to unwrap it to get the URL for the registry, and it means a non-image asset should be embedded with Roam's own syntax rather than the markdown `![]()` the source note used. (`roamAlphaAPI.util.uploadFile` is a legacy alias for the same call.) 9:- **The original filename is preserved, in Firebase custom metadata.** Verified against a real upload: requesting the Storage URL with `alt=media` **stripped** returns the object descriptor as JSON, and the uploaded name is in `metadata["file-name"]` (alongside `metadata["file-type"]`): 22:- **Roam never collects uploaded files, and says so.** Its documentation: "Deleting a block doesn't delete the file that was uploaded in it. The upload stays in your graph's storage… There's no way to search for those leftover files yet." So nothing upstream will clean up after us, and orphans are undiscoverable — which independently confirms what the API surface implies. The same page notes that deleting a file runs a **reference check** telling you whether anything still displays it, and that deletion is permanent. That check is a property of Roam's own deletion flow, not something `file.delete({url})` exposes to us. 61:- At publish time the Roam client fetches each referenced Firebase asset, hashes it, uploads it to the `assets` bucket through `addFile`, and writes a `FileReference` whose `filepath` is the Firebase URL exactly as it appears in the markdown. 70:- At import time the Roam client downloads the asset from the Supabase bucket with its authenticated client and re-uploads it via `file.upload`, then rewrites the markdown link to the returned URL. 81: - _We do not choose the location._ Obsidian picks the vault path, so it is stable and re-import is idempotent for free: the filesystem **is** the registry, resolved by `getFirstLinkpathDest`. Roam's `file.upload` assigns a fresh random URL on every call, so what the filesystem guarantees Obsidian for nothing, Roam has to be told. 100:- Before uploading, look up the hash and reuse the URL if present. 105:2. For each hash — if `assetRegistry` has it, reuse the URL. Otherwise upload, then record `hash -> url`. 109:**Why a registry at all:** `file.upload` is not idempotent. Without a memo, an asset referenced by three imported nodes becomes three Firebase blobs at three URLs, and every re-import adds another. Supabase already deduplicates by hash — one blob, N `FileReference` rows under different `filepath`s — so the mirror must key on **hash, not reference**, or it re-inflates what the bucket collapsed. Note this is about **not creating** garbage, which is a separate concern from collecting it (Decision 6). 111:- **Why the key is (graph, hash):** per-graph is inherent, since `file.upload` writes into the importing graph's own `imgs/app//` folder. Cross-graph duplication is therefore not avoidable and is arguably correct. 112:- **Name every upload `imported-.`.** 113:- Verified end to end: uploading a `File` named `imported-deadbeef.txt` and calling `file.get` on the returned URL yields `name: imported-deadbeef.txt`, and the name is separately readable from `metadata["file-name"]` without downloading the bytes (see Context). 126:- `file.upload` returns a bare URL for anything that is not an image, PDF, audio or video, and a bare URL in a Roam block renders as a link whose visible text **is** the URL — a hundred-odd characters of storage uid that tells the reader nothing. The rewriting step must therefore emit `[report.docx](url)`, taking the label from the source markdown's display text or the basename of its path, rather than dropping the returned URL in raw. The name is otherwise never surfaced anywhere in Roam: images render as images, media types render in a viewer, and `metadata["file-name"]` is read by nothing in the Roam UI. This link label is the only place a user ever sees what an imported file is called. (The bare-URL rendering is inferred from the reference, not observed — confirm against a real graph.) 135:Record `hash -> url` after the upload returns. 137:**Why not the reverse:** writing a placeholder before uploading was intended to make a crash between the two detectable. It does not help. The placeholder carries no URL, so a later sync can neither reuse the upload nor locate it — the outcome is a re-upload either way — and the stranded file is undiscoverable regardless, since Roam exposes no way to list a graph's files. The extra write buys a flag nothing can act on. 139:**Accepted cost:** a crash between upload and record leaves one orphaned file. It is invisible, permanent, and harmless apart from quota. This is the same class of residue Roam's own documentation treats as normal. 151:**Why leaving files behind is acceptable:** Roam does not collect them either, and says so — "Deleting a block doesn't delete the file that was uploaded in it. The upload stays in your graph's storage." Orphaned uploads are a normal, tolerated condition in this host, not a defect we are introducing. 180:- **Why 6 MiB on the publish side:** it is Supabase's threshold for a standard upload, above which an uploader is expected to switch to a resumable one, which `addFile` does not implement. It is also the number Obsidian's publisher already enforced, so the platforms stay symmetric: an asset publishable from Obsidian is publishable from Roam. It is deliberately **not** read from the bucket's own `file_size_limit` (50 MiB in `supabase/config.toml`), because the binding constraint is the upload method rather than what the bucket would accept. 181:- **Why the import side carries the same number in a separate constant:** the two answer different questions and are expected to diverge. The publish cap is about what we will store and pay for; the import cap is about what a browser should shuttle — down from Supabase and back up into the destination's storage, once per importing graph — and what it spends of that user's quota there. Roam's own upload ceiling is unknown to us. One figure to reason about for v0, two places to change when that stops being true. 183:- **ENG-1784's 5 MB does not apply here.** That is Vercel's request-payload limit on the AI-assisted extraction path. No Vercel function sits in either asset transfer: publishing hands bytes to Supabase Storage through `supabase-js`, and importing pushes them to `roamAlphaAPI.file.upload`, which is Roam's own backend. 192:- **`file.upload` returns a media-type-dependent block string, not a URL** → The mirror must unwrap `![](url)`, `{{[[pdf]]: url}}`, `{{[[audio]]: url}}`, `{{[[video]]: url}}` or a bare URL before storing it in the registry. It also means a non-image asset should be written into the page with Roam's own embed syntax rather than the markdown `![]()` the Obsidian source used — link rewriting is not a straight substitution for those types. 193:- **Both transfer directions need an explicit size cap, and neither can inherit one** → Today nothing above 6 MB reaches the bucket, so "mirror everything referenced" is a safe default on the import side. Once larger files can be published, that default commits the importing client to pulling each one out of Supabase and pushing it into Firebase, both in the browser, on every graph that imports the node — and it spends the user's Roam storage quota at that scale. Roam's own upload ceiling is unknown to us. The mirror needs an explicit cap of its own rather than an inherited one, and an asset over it should be reported and left as an unresolved reference, matching the existing degradation path. The publish direction (Decision 2) needs its own cap for the same reason and against a different limit — what we are willing to pull out of Firebase and store in our bucket, at our cost, rather than what Roam will accept. **Settled in Decision 9:** 6 MiB each, as two separate constants. 194:- **Roam could re-issue a Firebase download token** → The URL string would change, and a re-publish would write a second `FileReference` under a different primary key for bytes we already hold. Deduplication by `filehash` limits the cost to a redundant row rather than a redundant blob. Tokens are created at upload and do not rotate on their own, so this is recorded rather than guarded against. --- tests: 5: extractUploadedUrl, 6- mirrorAssetToRoamStorage, 7- mirroredAssetFileName, 8-} from "../mirrorAssetToRoamStorage"; 9-import { readMirroredAssetUrl, recordMirroredAsset } from "../assetRegistry"; -- 73:describe("extractUploadedUrl", () => { 74- // `file.upload` returns a media-type-dependent block string, not a URL. 75- it.each([ 76- ["an image", `![](${UPLOADED_URL})`], 77- ["an image with alt text", `![diagram](${UPLOADED_URL})`], -- 84: expect(extractUploadedUrl(uploadReturn)).toBe(UPLOADED_URL); 85- }); 86- 87- it("reports a shape it cannot read rather than guessing a URL", () => { 88- expect( 89: extractUploadedUrl("{{[[roam/render]]: something}}"), 90- ).toBeUndefined(); 91: expect(extractUploadedUrl("")).toBeUndefined(); 92- // A URL embedded in prose is not an upload result, so it is not taken. 93- expect( 94: extractUploadedUrl(`see ${UPLOADED_URL} for details`), 95- ).toBeUndefined(); 96- }); 97-}); 98-

Review: PR #1397 — mirrorAssetToRoamStorage

Scope: two new files (apps/roam/src/utils/mirrorAssetToRoamStorage.ts, plus its test). Verified: the suite passes (19/19), tsc --noEmit on apps/roam is clean, the bucket path (contentHash) matches what addFile writes, and storage.info()'s size/contentType are genuinely optional in @supabase/storage-js@2.105.4, so the !== undefined guard is correct.

Findings

- apps/roam/src/utils/mirrorAssetToRoamStorage.ts:61 (medium) — UPLOAD_RETURN_PATTERNS has no branch for [label](url), which is the form Roam writes for a non-media upload (a .docx, .zip, .txt). The sibling module findAssetReferences.ts:29 explicitly lists that form as one of "the forms Roam writes an uploaded file in". If file.upload returns it, extractUploadedUrl returns undefined and line 179 throws — after the bytes were already uploaded, so the graph gains an orphaned file, nothing is recorded, and every retry orphans another. Given the comment at line 64-68 already argues for tolerating the unobserved {{pdf: url}} shape by the same asymmetry, [label](url) is a stronger candidate for inclusion than the one that was included.
- apps/roam/src/utils/mirrorAssetToRoamStorage.ts:177 (low/medium) — file.upload({ file }) is called without toast: { hide: true } (the option exists in the typings, roamjs-components/types/index.d.ts:380). This function is designed for bulk import — one call per distinct asset hash across every imported node — so a 40-asset import fires 40 Roam upload toasts at the user. The existing call sites that omit it are single, user-initiated uploads, so their precedent doesn't carry here.
- apps/roam/src/utils/mirrorAssetToRoamStorage.ts:144 (medium) — if (infoError) throw infoError makes a purely optional pre-check fatal. The comment at 140-142 frames info as an optimisation ("one small request instead of the download"), and the code already handles info being absent or size-less (lines 153, 166 both use info?.). But an info failure — the object-info route unavailable, or a storage policy that permits download but not info — aborts the mirror for every asset even though the download path alone is sufficient and correct. Treating an infoError as "no metadata" and falling through to the post-download size check would preserve the cap and remove the failure mode.
- apps/roam/src/utils/mirrorAssetToRoamStorage.ts:134 (low/medium) — the readMirroredAssetUrl check is a synchronous read separated from recordMirroredAsset (line 184) by two awaits. A caller that mirrors assets concurrently (Promise.all over a node's assets, or over nodes sharing an asset) has every in-flight call see an empty registry for the same hash, so the same bytes upload N times, the registry keeps one URL, and N-1 blobs are orphaned in the user's Firebase quota. assetRegistry.ts prices in the lost-write case, but not the duplicate-upload case, and this is the module that could cheaply prevent it with a module-level Map<string, Promise<AssetMirrorResult>> of in-flight hashes.
- apps/roam/src/utils/mirrorAssetToRoamStorage.ts:100 (low) — extensionFor validates the mimetype-derived subtype against /^[a-z0-9]+$/i (line 105) but applies no validation at all to the filename-derived branch: it returns everything after the last dot verbatim. An Obsidian source_path like notes/2024.06.01 meeting (no extension, dots in the stem) yields the file name imported-<hash>.06.01 meeting — a spaced, meaningless extension uploaded to Roam — where the mimetype fallback would have produced the right one. Applying the same character check to the filename branch, and falling through to the mimetype when it fails, would fix it.
- apps/roam/src/utils/mirrorAssetToRoamStorage.ts:62 (low) — the embed branches capture (\S+) with no scheme check, so ![](not-a-url) would be extracted and recorded as the asset's URL. This contradicts the stated design at line 57-59 ("recording the wrong URL is worse than reporting an unknown shape") — only the bare-URL branch at line 70 enforces https?://. Requiring the scheme in all four branches (as findAssetReferences.ts:14's URL_PATTERN does) costs nothing.
- apps/roam/src/utils/mirrorAssetToRoamStorage.ts:28 (low) — SkippedAsset is exported here with the shape {contentHash, reason, size, limit}, while copyAssetToSharedStorage.ts:30 exports a different SkippedAsset with {sourceRef, sourcePath, reason, size, limit}. The import pipeline that consumes both (publish results and mirror results) will have to alias one at every import site, and a mistaken import type-checks in some positions since both are status: "skipped" with three shared fields. Naming this one SkippedMirror/SkippedImport avoids it.

Not findings (checked and clear)

Size cap semantics are consistently inclusive with the publish side; the post-download blob.size re-check correctly covers lying metadata; upload-then-record ordering is tested and correct; the bucket key matches addFile's hashvalue; download/info errors and a null blob are all handled before any upload.

**Two premises needed correcting first.**

Finding 1 says `[label](url)` "is the form Roam writes for a non-media upload". That's not what the evidence says: design.md:126 records `file.upload` returning a **bare URL** for anything that isn't image/PDF/audio/video, and the `[label](url)` line in `findAssetReferences.ts:29` is about page content — its own comment says "a plain markdown link covers a file a user linked rather than embedded", and it's also the form *our* rewriter emits. So non-media returns are already covered by the bare-URL branch.

The finding still lands on its second argument, which is the stronger one: an unreadable return throws *after* the upload, so it costs an orphaned blob plus an unresolved asset, and every retry orphans another. I added the branch on that basis and rewrote the header comment to say which branches are observed and which are tolerance — the previous wording implied all five were documented returns.

**Applied**

- **6** — every branch now requires `https?://` via a shared `UPLOADED_URL` fragment, so `![](not-a-url)` no longer resolves. Four new refusal cases.
- **1** — `[label](url)` branch added, safe because of 6.
- **3** — `storage.info` failure is treated as absent metadata rather than fatal. Two tests: mirrors on when info fails, and still refuses an over-cap asset in that case via the post-download check.
- **5** — the filename-derived extension is now validated with the same `EXTENSION_CHARACTERS` test as the MIME-derived one, falling through when it fails. `notes/2024.06.01 meeting` + `application/pdf` now yields `imported-<hash>.pdf`.
- **2** — `toast: { hide: true }`, asserted in a test.
- **7** — `SkippedAsset` → `SkippedMirror`. No other module imported it, so the rename is local.

**Declined — 4 (in-flight promise map).** No caller mirrors concurrently: this branch has no caller at all, and the one on eng-2219 loops sequentially with a comment saying it does so precisely to keep the registry check meaningful. Adding a dedupe map now guards a caller that doesn't exist, and it wouldn't help across two tabs, which is the only concurrency a real graph sees. If a caller ever parallelizes, this module is the right place for it — but that change belongs with that caller.

Applied both. `tsc --noEmit` clean, 32 files / 281 tests pass; rewrite suite now 26.

**1 — declared kind captured.** Branches 3 and 4 now capture the media keyword, and it enters `kindOf` as `declaredKind` on a `ReferenceContext`, ranked directly under the recorded MIME type and above every guess. `{{[[pdf]]: <uid-url>}}` stays a PDF; `{{audio: …}}` comes back as `{{[[audio]]: …}}`. The ordering now reads as decreasing commitment by the source: MIME → declared → extension → form.

**2 — fallback narrowed, list extended.** `embed → image` applies only when neither name carries an extension at all. Added `avif`, `heic`, `tiff`, `ico`, `flac`, `aac`, `m4v`, `mkv`, `avi`. So `![[photo.avif]]` embeds on its extension, an extension-less storage URL embeds on its form, and `![[notes/report.docx]]` is a labelled link again with its name intact.

One existing test changed expectation rather than staying green: `![](vault/odd.constructor)` now yields `[odd.constructor](url)` instead of `![](url)`. That's the new rule working — an unknown extension is a `file` — and the test still does its real job, so I renamed it and added a comment saying the point is that the literal `undefined` never reaches the page, not the embed form.

Two new regression tests cover exactly the cases you named: the declared-kind media embeds, and the non-media wikilink embed keeping its label.

content.text:
Yes — one place, in `labelFor`, since the visible symptom is the label rather than the kind.

Worth narrowing the case first, though: for a Roam-origin asset `copyAssetToSharedStorage` records `source_path` from the descriptor's `file-name` metadata, so most such rows *do* carry a real name with an extension, and both the kind and the label come out right. The residual case needs `source_path` to be absent or itself extension-less — which happens when the descriptor had no `file-name` and the publisher fell back to the storage uid (task 2.2's fallback), or on any row written before that column existed.
